planting.note: Plant a grafted bare-root or container tree in early spring on well-drained soil in full sun, and site a compatible sweet cherry pollinizer nearby since fruit set improves markedly with cross-pollination.

directions: 0900 Ziraat is a Turkish-bred sweet cherry selection, named for its original agricultural research registration number, that became one of the world's most widely planted commercial sweet cherry cultivars thanks to its large, firm, dark-red fruit and reliable productivity. The heart-shaped cherries ripen mid-season and ship well, which has carried the cultivar from its home orchards in Turkey into commercial plantings in Washington State, California, Chile, and parts of southern Europe. Give trees deep, well-drained soil and consistent moisture during fruit swell, since inconsistent watering close to harvest can cause fruit cracking in this thin-skinned type. Prune for an open center to let light into the canopy and keep fruiting wood renewed, as cherries set best on young spurs rather than old wood.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit — sweet cherry cultivar evaluations

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Kabaaşı blooms early like other Malatya apricots, so a sheltered site away from late-frost pockets protects the crop.

directions: Kabaaşı is one of the principal apricot cultivars grown alongside Hacıhaliloğlu in the Malatya basin of eastern Turkey, the region that supplies most of the world's dried apricots. Fruit is medium-to-large with orange skin and a light blush, freestone, and sweet enough for fresh eating but grown mainly for the region's traditional sun-drying trays laid out across hillside terraces each summer. Like other Malatya apricots, it blooms early and is vulnerable to spring frost, so growers favor elevated or air-drained sites that reduce cold-pocket risk during flowering. Trees need a true winter chill to break dormancy evenly and perform best with deep, infrequent watering once established rather than constantly moist soil.
sources: Malatya Apricot Research Institute (Türkiye)

common_name: Papazkarası Grape (Turkish Thracian Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Root hardwood cuttings or plant bench-grafted vines in spring on a trellis in full sun; Papazkarası is a vigorous, productive variety that benefits from moderate cluster thinning to concentrate flavor.

directions: Papazkarası is an indigenous red wine grape of Turkey's Thracian region around Tekirdağ, its name translating roughly to 'priest's black,' a nod to the variety's long association with the region's old monastic and village wine-making traditions. The grape produces light-bodied, lower-tannin red wines and is often blended with other Thracian reds rather than bottled as a single-variety wine, reflecting its traditional role as an everyday table-wine grape. Vines are vigorous and reliably productive on the Marmara region's clay-limestone soils, tolerating the area's humid summers reasonably well compared to more disease-prone varieties. Train on a trellis with good air circulation and thin crowded clusters in midsummer to help ripening and reduce fungal pressure in wetter years.
sources: Tekirdağ Viticulture Research Institute (Türkiye)

common_name: Kunduru Durum Wheat (Anatolian Hard Wheat Landrace)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast seed into tilled ground in mid-to-late fall across Western Anatolia's winter-wheat belt, letting plants establish before dormancy and resume growth with spring warmth.

directions: Kunduru is a long-standing durum (hard amber) wheat landrace type from the Aegean and Central Anatolian regions of Turkey, selected and stabilized into registered lines such as the historic 'Kunduru 1149' for its glassy, high-protein kernels suited to bulgur, pasta, and traditional tarhana. Plants tiller well on rainfed ground and tolerate the dry, hot Anatolian summer that follows a cool, wet winter growing season, making it well matched to a Mediterranean-type dryland wheat climate. Sow into a firm seedbed in autumn and avoid excess nitrogen, which encourages lodging in this relatively tall-strawed landrace type compared to modern semi-dwarf durums. Harvest when heads are fully dry and hard for the best milling quality, since durum's hard endosperm needs full field-drying rather than early cutting.
sources: Morgounov et al., 'Wheat Landraces Currently Grown in Turkey: Distribution, Diversity, and Use', Crop Science, 2016
Republic of Turkey Bahri Dağdaş International Agricultural Research Institute — Wheat Landraces Inventory of Turkey

common_name: Prokupac Grape (Serbian Indigenous Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or bench grafts in spring on a trellis in full sun; Prokupac is late-ripening and productive, so site it on a warm south-facing slope where the season runs long enough to finish.

directions: Prokupac is considered Serbia's oldest native wine grape, taking its name from the southern town of Prokuplje in the Toplica River valley where it has been cultivated for centuries as the backbone of the region's everyday red and rosé wines. Bunches are large and loose with moderate tannin and acidity, traditionally fermented into light, fruity table wine but increasingly used by modern Serbian winemakers for more structured single-variety reds and rosés. The vine is vigorous and late-ripening, so it needs a long warm season and benefits from a south-facing slope with good drainage in cooler Balkan microclimates. Prune to an open canopy to help its naturally dense growth ripen fully and to reduce humidity-driven disease pressure around the clusters.
sources: Serbia Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Water Management — indigenous grape variety register

common_name: Vranac Grape (Montenegrin Indigenous Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or grafted vines in spring on a trellis in full sun; Vranac is late-ripening and wants a long, hot Mediterranean-adjacent season to fully soften its heavy tannins.

directions: Vranac, whose name means 'black stallion,' is Montenegro's flagship native red wine grape and is also widely grown across neighboring Macedonia, producing deeply colored, full-bodied, tannic red wines traditionally centered on the Skadar Lake basin near Podgorica. The grape is late-ripening and needs the long, hot summers of the sub-Mediterranean valleys where it is traditionally grown, with some of the world's largest single plantings found on the plain south of Podgorica. Clusters are medium-sized and tight, requiring careful canopy management to maintain airflow and avoid rot in years with late-season rain. Because the wine's character depends on full phenolic ripeness, growers commonly delay harvest well into autumn to let tannins soften before picking.

common_name: Devzira Rice (Fergana Valley Uzbek Plov Rice)

planting.note: Transplant seedlings or direct sow into a warm, flooded bed well after soil has warmed; Devzira is traditionally grown in mineral-rich Fergana Valley soils and benefits from standing water through tillering.

directions: Devzira is a prized traditional Uzbek rice landrace from the Fergana Valley, distinguished by an unpolished reddish-pink bran layer that tints cooking liquid and finished rice a faint rosy hue while adding a distinctly nutty, slightly chewy texture. It is considered the premium choice for Uzbek plov, where cooks value the way its grains absorb fat and broth without turning mushy, and it commands a price well above ordinary rice in Central Asian markets. The crop is grown in flooded paddy-style beds much like other irrigated rices, needing full sun, steady warmth, and consistent standing water through the vegetative season to fill out its grain properly. Because it is a long-season landrace rather than a modern high-yield variety, expect lower yields and taller, more lodging-prone plants than commercial short-grain rice.
sources: Uzbekistan Rice Research Institute

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings on a sturdy trellis in spring in full sun; Nimrang is a very late-season table grape that needs a long, hot growing period to fill out its large berries.

directions: Nimrang is a classic Central Asian table grape long grown across Uzbekistan and neighboring Tajikistan, known for its large, elongated, amber-green to pink-blushed berries carried in long, loose clusters. The variety is prized above all for its exceptional keeping quality, since growers traditionally hang whole bunches in cool, dry storage rooms to eat fresh well into the winter months after harvest. It was also used as parent breeding stock in Soviet-era Central Asian table grape programs for its size, storage life, and late ripening habit. Vines need a long, hot season and lean, well-drained soil, and growers typically thin clusters to encourage larger individual berries on the remaining fruit.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings on a trellis in spring in full sun; this old Central Asian variety needs a long, hot season to fully size its distinctive elongated berries.

directions: Husayne is an old Central Asian table grape, historically grown across Afghanistan and Turkestan, prized for its striking long, finger-shaped amber berries carried in large loose clusters. Introduced to American growers in the early twentieth century, it became known in California as the 'Lady Finger' grape, valued for its crisp texture and mild, sweet flavor as much as its unusual shape. The vine is vigorous and needs a long, hot growing season to size and ripen its elongated berries fully, performing best on lean, well-drained soil similar to its native arid-region habitat. It remains more of a heritage dooryard grape than a commercial variety today, grown by collectors and in germplasm collections for its history and novelty.
sources: U.P. Hedrick, 'The Grapes of New York', New York Agricultural Experiment Station, 1908
